blocks.text: Its lung, namely, is very large. Pliny, book 11, chapter 37: The chameleon has a lung very large in proportion, and nothing else inside. Plutarch, in the book Utra anim.: Συνέπεται δὲ καὶ πνεύματος πλῆθος, ὡς Θεόφραστος. Ὀλίγον γὰρ ἀποδεῖ πᾶν τὸ σῶμα τοῦ ζώου πλῆρες εἶναι πνεύμονος, ᾧ τεκμαίρεται τὸ πνευματικὸν αὐτοῦ [synepetai de kai pneumatos plēthos, hōs Theophrastos. Oligon gar apodei pan to sōma tou zōou plēres einai pneumonos, hō tekmairetai to pneumatikon autou]; There is also an abundance of breath in it, as Theophrastus reports. For the whole body is very nearly full of lung, from which he infers how full of air it is. Belon: Since it is furnished with large lungs extending along the sides of the belly, it draws air inward with great force and swells up ^{(1)}. Tertullian [II, 506] in the book De pallio: It feeds by gaping, ruminates by puffing like bellows; its food comes from the wind, etc. But, what is more surprising, it is also believed to go on breathing for a long time after being dissected. The Philosopher, in that excellent description of the chameleon in book 2, chapter 11 of the History: Ἐνεργεῖ δὲ καὶ τῷ πνεύματι, ἀνατετμημένος ὅλος ἐπὶ πολὺν χρόνον, βραχείας ἰσχυρῶς ἔτι κινήσεως ἐν αὐτῷ περὶ τὴν καρδίαν οὔσης [energei de kai tō pneumati, anatetmēmenos holos epi polyn chronon, bracheias ischyrōs eti kinēseōs en autō peri tēn kardian ousēs]; Even when it has been dissected entirely, it retains the power of breath for a long time, that is, as long as some motion, however slight, remains around the heart. This breath is called in Arabic نسيم [nasīm] nasim, from the very root from which its name תנשמת thinsemeth comes. Damir: يغتذي بالنسيم ويعيش بالبرد الهوا [yaghtadhī bi-l-nasīm wa-yaʿīsh bi-l-bard al-hawā] It is nourished by τῷ [tō] nasim (that is, by breath) and feeds on cold air. Yet by a very great error he transfers this to the land crocodile, as we noted above ^{b)}, although it is proper to the chameleon. And yet it is not quite truly written that the chameleon lives on air alone. For it has a very long tongue, sticky at the tip, by darting which it catches flies and gnats from the branch of the tree on which it sits. Damir: لسانه طويل جدا مقدار [col. 1081] ذراع وذلك دليل علي انه يكون مطوي في حلقه وهو يبلع ما بعد عنه من الذباب [lisānuhu ṭawīl jiddan miqdār dhirāʿ wa-dhālika dalīl ʿalā annahu yakūn maṭwī fī ḥalqihi wa-huwa yablaʿ mā baʿuda ʿanhu min al-dhubāb] Its tongue is very long, namely a cubit in measure. Accordingly it keeps it folded in its throat, and shoots it out in order to (catch and) eat flies that are at a distance from it. Algazel in the Mirabilia: والحربا خلق الله لسانها بخلاف المعتاد لتلحق به ما بعد عنها بثلاث اشبار ونحوه وتصتاد به علي هذه المسافة [wa-l-ḥirbā khalaqa Allāh lisānahā bi-khilāf al-muʿtād li-talḥaqa bihi mā baʿuda ʿanhā bi-thalāth ashbār wa-naḥwihi wa-taṣtād bihi ʿalā hādhihi al-masāfa] God created for the chameleon a tongue quite different from the usual, so that with it it might reach things about three spans away from it, and hunt what lies within this distance. Johannes Landius, cited by Scaliger, supports the Arabs: he says that when he was in farthest Syria he saw one of the five chameleons he had bought pick off, by a sudden, instantaneous dart of its tongue, a fly that was on its breast. And Belon, who had seen them alive in Egypt and Arabia: It has a round tongue, a palm and a half long, which it darts from afar at the insects on which it chiefly feeds; and with the spongy slime it has at the tip it draws flies, beetles, locusts and ants to itself ^{(2)}. Hence its name حربا [ḥirbā] chirba, as if one were to say the darter. For حربة [ḥarba] charba is a kind of javelin or short lance. Accordingly the herb lonchitis, whose seed resembles the point of a lance, is called in Arabic حربة [ḥarba] [II, 507] charba ^{(3)}. But why it is called χαμαιλέων [chamaileōn] in Greek is less clear, since this most sluggish and timid animal seems to have scarcely anything in common with the lion. Tertullian, in the place cited above: When you hear of a chameleon, not knowing it before, you will at once fear something more than a lion. But when you come upon it in a vineyard, almost entirely under a vine leaf, you will immediately laugh at the boldness of the name. Yet by the Arab poets too it is called باقرة [bāqira] bakira, that is, lioness. For with them باقر [bāqir] bakir is lion. And an animalcule similar to the chameleon is called ليث عفرين [layth ʿIfrīn] lion of Iphrin, from the place where it is born. Alcamus: ليث عفرين دابة كالحربا يتعرض للراكب ويضربه بذنبه [layth ʿIfrīn dābba ka-l-ḥirbā yataʿarraḍ li-l-rākib wa-yaḍribuhu bi-dhanabihi] The lion of Iphrin, an animal like the chameleon, which attacks a rider and strikes him with its tail. So it is rightly called a lion, since in a chameleon's body it has a lion's spirit. Accordingly, if it were established that this animal was known to the Greeks, I would say that the name chameleon was first given to it and afterwards transferred to the other, similar animal. But since none of the ancients mentions this animalcule, it seems to me more probable that, just as the Arabs call the chameleon جمل [jamal] gemel, or جمل يهود [jamal yahūd] gemel jehoud, that is, the Jewish camel, as Damir and Abenbitar report, so the Phoenicians in Africa called it גמל gamal, or גמליון gamalion, from which the word χαμαιλέων [chamaileōn] was formed, inflected in the Greek manner so that it would seem [II, 508] to be Greek. Nor is it obscure why the Arabs called it a camel. For, just as they attribute to it the head of a calf, the body of a little fish and the feet of a gecko, so too, in Damir, سنام [col. 1082] البعير [sanām al-baʿīr] the hump of a camel, because like a camel it has a humped back. There are also those who call it مجوسي [majūsī], that is, a Magian or Magusaean, because it seems to worship the sun, since it is constantly turned towards it. It is said to change hour by hour, according as the sunlight is stronger or its heat more intense: in the morning it is ash-grey, then yellow, and finally green when the sun is hottest ^{(4)}. But in fear too, or if something is put in its way, it takes on other colours. Hence the proverb about one who does not remain in the same state: تلون الحرباء [talawwana al-ḥirbāʾ] The chameleon has changed colour. So Alcibiades was once called χαμαιλέοντος εὐμεταβολώτερος [chamaileontos eumetabolōteros], more changeable than a chameleon. The Arabs forbid eating it, because it is venomous and a species of وزغ [wazagh] guezga, or gecko. In Avicenna and Abenbitar, its blood removes the hair of the eyelids. In Damir, its gall removes dimness of sight, and its fat is applied to ulcers and scars. In Alkazuini, remedies from the chameleon are prescribed against epilepsy, hail, locusts and enchantment. But to dwell on these any longer is not a matter for our leisure.
